covering.note: Its skin is brown or black, sometimes with dark orange spots.

size.note: It weighs 405 g to 1 kg and is 30 to 69 cm long.

diet.note: It mostly eats crayfish, plus fish, tadpoles and insects.

trees.note: It hides under flat rocks and never climbs.

lifespan.note: It can live up to 30 years.

clues.text: Its head and body are very flat, and it has no eyelids.
Loose, wrinkly folds of skin along its sides help it breathe through its skin.
Its big tail is shaped like a paddle, flat from side to side.
As an adult it has no gills on the outside, just one gill slit on each side of its head.
It sees poorly. It senses movement in the water and smells its prey.
By day it hides under a big flat rock on the stream bed, and it defends that rock from other hellbenders.
It lives its whole life in the water.
Its skin is very slimy, and the slime puts off many predators.
The father digs a nest under a rock and guards the eggs.
It needs clear, cool, fast-flowing streams, and avoids water warmer than 20 °C.
Mud washing in from logging, mining and roads buries the rocks it needs for shelter and nests.

facts.text: It is the largest salamander in North America.
Its nicknames include "snot otter" and "lasagna lizard".
Its closest relatives are the giant salamanders of China and Japan.
Many anglers think it is poisonous and cut their line rather than unhook one.
It takes in about 90% of its oxygen through its skin, so it needs water rich in oxygen.
A male can rock back and forth to move fresh water over its skin.
Other hellbenders often eat its eggs and young, so the father guards the nest against them.
Eggs hatch after 45 to 80 days, and young hellbenders take 5 to 8 years to grow up.
Several females may lay in the same nest: over 1,900 eggs have been found in one.
Dams stop the fast flow of the streams it lives in.
Traces of its DNA in the water show it is gone from over a third of the West Virginia sites where it once lived. Runoff from roads is a likely cause.
